blocks.text: At the Blackwells’ home, Eleanor had told Billy to leave Daniel alone. Later, he had found his aunt beside the Defender editor’s telephone. Their conversation there had ended without an explanation for the call that had put Daniel’s cleanup claim in the paper. Neither her warning nor her visit was proof that she had helped pay for a robot. Eleanor knew it, and Billy knew she knew it.

After the robot attack, police had searched Daniel’s upstairs laboratory and found him gone. Now its shutters were down. Billy stood across from the building, looking at the neighboring doors instead. Somebody owned it. Somebody collected the rent.

The first address in an old city directory led to a locked office. A repairman at the next building remembered a different agent, but his number had been disconnected. Billy spent two afternoons following property records and old telephone listings before the owner of a hardware shop finally directed him to the landlord’s office out back.
By the time Billy reached the little office, the man inside was closing for the day.
The landlord was broad-shouldered, with a gray beard and a face that suggested he had already been disappointed by three people that afternoon. He kept one hand on the office door.
“What do you want with Orkleson?” he asked.
“We went to school together,” Billy said.
“Good. Tell your old schoolmate the rent’s due. That Blackwell lady can afford it.”

blocks.alt: Inspector Billy, a short stocky private investigator with his face hidden by a high coat collar and plaid cap, questions a gruff gray-bearded landlord outside his modest Cleveland office.
blocks.text: Billy kept his pencil still. “Which Blackwell lady?” The landlord squinted at him. “Silver hair. Dark glasses. Eleanor, I think. She never seemed short of money until this month.”
“Eleanor Blackwell is my aunt,” Billy said. “If you have a copy of the invoice, I’ll take it to her.”

The landlord held the door halfway shut. “I shouldn’t hand an account to a man who walks in off the street.” He glanced back at the unpaid figure on his desk. A month’s rent mattered more to him than asking whether Billy had any right to see the page. “You can put it in her hand?”
“I can.”

The landlord fetched the carbon copy. The invoice named Daniel Orkleson as the tenant at the laboratory address and Eleanor Blackwell as the person billed. Beneath the amount due, it listed several earlier months paid under her name. The landlord tapped the latest line. “She used to send it by driver. Once she brought it herself. Tell her this one’s late.”

Billy folded the invoice into his notebook. One page showed who had been paying for Daniel’s laboratory. It did not show what Eleanor knew about the robot, but it was finally something Jenny could check.

At the Defender, Jenny was arranging interview questions when Billy came through the newsroom. Her editor had sent her to cover Eleanor’s campaign launch. In less than an hour, she was due to speak with the prospective candidate before the public announcement at Cleveland City Hall.

Billy laid the invoice on the corner of her desk, away from the other reporters. Jenny read the name, then read it again. She asked where he had found it and whether the landlord would confirm the payment history. Billy gave her every step, including the doors that had gone nowhere.

blocks.alt: In the 1987 Cleveland Defender newsroom, Billy quietly shows Jenny, in her civilian reporter clothes, one itemized laboratory rent invoice naming Eleanor Blackwell while typewriters and desks fill the background.
blocks.text: Jenny pressed the invoice flat beneath her hand. “If this isn’t true, I’ll be fired. The Blackwell name means something in this city. Claude has done good work here, and I won’t drag him into a story about Eleanor without a reason.”
“The invoice names her,” Billy said. “Not him.”

“I see that. I’m asking her about it. Then I’m checking every line before a word goes to print.” She made a copy for the newsroom and handed Billy’s back to him. “Did she know what Daniel was building?”
“I don’t know. But officers were told to hold back when his equipment was at the lake. If she wins the mayor’s office and she’s still protecting him, he could do whatever he likes in this city.”
Jenny looked at the empty space on her question sheet. She wrote Daniel Orkleson there, underlined it once, and went to keep her appointment.

City Hall was busy with cameras, aides and people hoping for a first look at the campaign. Eleanor received Jenny in a small room off the main hall. Her silver curls were neat; dark glasses hid her eyes. She answered questions about streets, repairs and public safety without once looking at the notes Jenny held.
“The robot damaged Superior Avenue,” Jenny said. “Daniel Orkleson built it. What would you have done when it reached the street?”
“I would have expected the police to stop it,” Eleanor said.
“They hadn’t arrived when the Defenders pulled people out of its path.”
Eleanor straightened a page that was already straight. “I’m glad no more people were hurt. But we can’t have vigilantes making their own rules for Cleveland.”
“Would that include the people who stopped Orkleson’s machine?”
Her smile tightened. “If they show up again and interfere with police work, I may have them arrested.”

Jenny felt heat rise in her face. She thought of Seth holding up the falling beam, of Fist driving Luke away, of Perch trapped behind glass. She kept her voice even. “People saw those same figures saving lives. Would you ask the police why they were held back?”
“I would ask for a full account,” Eleanor said. “From everyone involved.”
Jenny wrote that down. Then she asked the question she had brought in her folder. “Have you been paying the rent on Daniel Orkleson’s laboratory?”

For the first time, Eleanor paused. She turned one pearl earring between her fingers. “No. People send bills to the Blackwells all the time, Miss Jenkins. Some hope we’ll pay without asking questions. My name on an invoice doesn’t mean I paid it.”
“This one lists earlier rent payments under your name,” Jenny said. “Can you explain those?”
“Send it to my office. I won’t answer for a document I haven’t seen.”
“Will they answer today?” Jenny asked.
An aide opened the door. The announcement was starting. Eleanor rose. “You may send them your questions.”
Jenny had a denial, but no explanation for the payments on the page. She wrote down Eleanor’s exact words before following her into the hall.

blocks.alt: Eleanor Blackwell announces her Cleveland mayoral campaign at City Hall in 1987 while civilian reporter Jenny Jenkins takes composed notes despite anger, and Billy watches from the back of the gathering.
blocks.text: Outside Cleveland City Hall, Eleanor faced the cameras and announced that she would run for mayor. Applause rose around Jenny. Billy stood at the back of the crowd, watching his aunt promise a safer city.

Jenny closed her notebook on the promise. She would report the arrest threat, confirm the invoice with the landlord, and give Eleanor’s office a chance to answer. Beside the steps, Billy waited until his aunt came past and handed her the overdue bill. Eleanor glanced at her name, folded the page and put it away without asking how he had found it. As she turned back toward the cameras, Billy thought of Daniel somewhere in Cleveland, still free. If Eleanor won, the man who had built the robot might have City Hall clearing his path.
